passage:
I'm Sharmila, and I've watched my brother Harish on our Sunday family calls for about six months. When Dad starts on politics, Harish says "hmm" and looks somewhere else. He never argues. Then he goes on mute and sometimes his camera turns off. A few weeks ago he began missing the calls, saying he had work.

I can't say for sure what's going on inside him. Maybe he's tired, maybe he simply doesn't care. But on the last call Mum asked where he was, and Dad said, "He's always busy nowadays," in a small voice. I think the silence kept the calls peaceful, and I also think it's quietly costing the calls something.

qa.q: What did Harish say when Dad started on politics?
qa.a: Harish says "hmm" and looks somewhere else.

qa.q: What might Sharmila think Harish is feeling, and how sure is Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila suspects Harish may be tired or withdrawn but admits it cannot be said for sure what is going on inside.

qa.q: What could Harish do instead of staying silent, and why?
qa.a: Harish could say briefly that he disagrees or prefers a different topic, because a small honest remark may avoid building resentment and the missed calls.

qa.q: How might Dad feel when he says Harish is always busy nowadays?
qa.a: Dad sounds hurt and a little lonely, in a small voice, as the missing calls suggest distance he may not fully understand.

grounding: To avoid conflict the young adult never speaks, then withdraws from family calls, so peace on the surface weakens the relationship.

passage:
January, Sunday lunch. Uday Mama spends half an hour on how young people vote 'without thinking'. Sharmila, twenty-one, disagrees with almost all of it. She says nothing, smiles, passes the dal, and grips her glass so hard her knuckles go pale.
March, the family video call. Uday Mama starts again. Sharmila mutes herself, turns off her camera and says her internet is weak. She spends the call scrolling, jaw tight, rehearsing everything she will never say.
June. Her mother mentions that Mama asked why Sharmila never talks to him any more. Sharmila says she's busy. She has skipped the last three calls and a family lunch. When Mama sends a birthday message, she replies with a thumbs-up and nothing else. There was never a single argument. But something between them has quietly worn thin, and neither of them knows how to fix it.

qa.q: What does Sharmila say during the March video call?
What do Sharmila's pale knuckles in January suggest?
qa.a: She is angry and holding it in, keeping quiet on the outside while resentment builds.

qa.q: What could Sharmila try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Share one view calmly, or tell Mama privately that these talks upset her, so the relationship does not quietly wear thin.

qa.q: How might Uday Mama see Sharmila's silence?
qa.a: Mama may be confused and hurt, noticing she no longer talks to him without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying silent to avoid conflict, growing irritated and withdrawing from family calls until the relationship weakens.

passage:
Farhan, you're saying you'll just stay quiet with your Abbu from now on. I understand. Let Siddharth, your old neighbour, tell you what my silence cost me.
When I was twenty, my father and I disagreed about almost everything political. He'd talk at dinner and I'd say nothing. I told myself I was keeping the peace.
But I wasn't peaceful. I was boiling. I started eating in my room. I stopped calling when I moved to Pune for work. When he rang, I kept it to two minutes: 'Fine, Papa. Busy, Papa.' There was never one big fight. Just years of small silences.
He fell ill when I was twenty-eight. In the hospital he said, 'You never tell me what you think any more. I miss arguing with you.'
I had thought silence was respect. He had felt it as distance.
So, Farhan. You don't have to fight. But don't disappear. Say one true thing, gently, and stay at the table.

qa.q: How long did young Siddharth keep the phone calls with Papa?
How did young Siddharth feel at those dinners?
qa.a: Boiling with resentment inside, while believing that silence kept the peace.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept Siddharth and Papa closer?
qa.a: Sharing one true view gently at dinner and staying at the table, instead of retreating into silence and short calls.

qa.q: How did Siddharth's father feel about the silence?
qa.a: He felt it as distance and missed hearing his child's views, even the arguments.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding political conflict through silence, growing resentful and withdrawing, while the relationship quietly weakens.
